executive_assessment.text: Highland examples distinguish Oruro/Potosí Indigenous farming, ayllu governance and irrigation maintenance; urban water evidence concerns historical La Paz/El Alto droughts.
Wildfire evidence identifies named lowland Indigenous territories and San Ignacio de Velasco water constraints. Ayoreo protection risks are conditional and require non-contact safeguards.

Camiri/Kaami planning and WFP Oruro evaluation summaries provide capacities and limits; participation, spending allocations and short-term consumption protection do not establish lasting resilience or peace effects.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2026-02 reports: In southeastern Oruro and northern Potosí, models project drier dry seasons and wetter wet seasons with more floods and droughts; Quechua and Aymara highland farmers rely on rainfed or small-irrigation systems.

Source dated 2026-02 reports: The report attributes the 2023 highland drought to climate-related heat and El Niño: water flows fell one-third, and crop losses affected nearly two million farmers across seven departments including Oruro and Potosí.

Source dated 2026-02 reports: By 2023, visited irrigation systems remained operational under local maintenance; participating farmers continued selling crops during drought while neighboring rainfed communities struggled.

Source dated 2026-02 reports: Only two of six municipalities ratified project land-use plans, and turnover weakened their use; ayllu bylaws remained active for land management and resolving disputes with neighboring communities.
Source dated 2025-05-30 reports: Over 2.5 million hectares burned in lowland Indigenous territories; Chiquitanía fires consumed 92% of forest in Guarayo, Monte Verde and Pantanal territories.

Source dated 2025-05-30 reports: San Ignacio de Velasco Chiquitano communities faced fire-worsened water scarcity, reduced flows from private dams, agrochemical contamination and reportedly unenforced drought rules.

REDESCA's 2025 report says 2024 fires threatened Ayoreo people in voluntary isolation in the Chaco. It warns habitat destruction could force unwanted outside contact, exposing people to disease and violence; the extent of damage to uncontacted Ayoreo territory was unknown.
Source dated 2025-05-30 reports: Fire-season reports described pressure, invasion and disputes over Indigenous lands in Santa Cruz.
Source dated 2026-07 reports: In 2016–2017, rainfall deficits reached 36% in La Paz–El Alto; 256,000 people in 100 La Paz neighborhoods and seven El Alto districts faced water rationing.

Source dated 2026-07 reports: The 2022–2023 drought was meteorologically longer and more intense than 2016–2017, yet EPSAS reported no service restrictions or cuts after its drought protocol and system measures.

Source dated not stated reports: UNDP identifies underrepresentation of Indigenous views in Lifesystems plans and no established pathway to integrate hyperlocal priorities into municipal PTDIs and national adaptation planning.

Source dated not stated reports: Camiri allocated a budget to connect Kaami's plan with municipal planning; workshops engaged 16 of 19 Chaco Indigenous communities and produced a co-designed 3D map for the municipal planning process.

Source dated 2026-04-17 reports: WFP's Oruro intervention addressed rural poverty and water scarcity affecting climate-vulnerable smallholder subsistence producers and Indigenous communities through cash transfers and water-related productive assets.

Source dated 2026-04-17 reports: WFP's synopsis says cash transfers protected consumption after climate shocks, while their contribution to longer-term resilience remained unclear; it describes Urus water-access results as significant but needing better tailoring.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification or human approval. 16 of 16 evidence records and 1 of 1 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.

No reviewed primary source establishes armed conflict or organized violence disrupting climate-adaptation delivery in Bolivia; documented social conflict and land disputes are localized and not evidence of climate-caused violence.

REDESCA's 2024 wildfire mission is not representative and does not establish climate-change attribution for ignition; its Ayoreo forced-contact pathway is a conditional risk, not an observed violence event.

The full WFP evaluation PDF required JavaScript bot verification, and the FAO 2025 Oruro–Potosí anticipatory-action PDF exceeded the reader's size limit; claims rely only on accessible official page text or other opened reports.

The UNDP 2021 Oruro resilience report PDF returned 403; no claim relies on its body. The World Bank EVAs findings are based on project evaluations and 2023 site visits, with limited replication and municipal-plan continuity.
The Ayoreo pathway is a conditional protection risk grounded in REDESCA, not a report of unwanted contact or observed violence; prevention must respect non-contact.
A generic drought-crisis/social-conflict illustration is not treated as a demonstrated urban conflict pathway.
